item.title: Global stocks are mixed as AI shares tumble after a retreat on Wall Street
item.description: World stocks were mixed on Wednesday after a wave of heavy selling of stocks linked to artificial intelligence once again hit Wall Street.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street closed moderately lower Wednesday after another punishing pullback in AI stocks lost momentum as the day went on, reversing much of the market’s losses. The S&P 500 index fell 0.3 per cent after having been down as much as 3.2 per cent earlier in the day. The Nasdaq composite finished 0.6 per cent lower. At one point, it had been down as much as 4.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3 per cent. The market pared its losses even as a report raised more worries about high inflation and as President Donald Trump plans to escalate the U.S. trade war with major trading partners. AI stocks lost ground for a second day following Monday’s relief rally over the surprise reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Stocks have been generally falling since setting an all-time high last month as worries grow that AI stock prices have grown unjustifiably high. The market turnaround came as some of the biggest tech companies bounced back from steep drops. Nvidia, which was down more than nine per cent at one point, closed with a 3.9 per cent loss. Broadcom, which had dropped more than six per cent, ended just 0.1 per cent lower, while Microsoft came back from a more than 3 per cent slide to finish down 1.2 per cent. There were some gainers among tech stocks: Meta climbed 3.4 per cent and Salesforce rose 2 per cent. Gains in financial services stocks also helped temper the market’s losses. Visa rose 1.8 per cent, Mastercard gained 1.9 per cent and American Express rose 1.2 per cent. Anthropic bounced back from an early drop to close with a 1.1 per cent gain. Still, since soaring to US$115 per share on the day it became the first major frontier lab to go public, Anthropic shares have tumbled by about 28 per cent. Roughly three quarters of the stocks in the S&P 500 rose, although the pullback in technology stocks kept the index in the red. Technology companies, particularly those focused on AI, have large market values that give them a dominant influence over whether major indexes rise or fall. Nvidia is among the most valuable companies on Wall Street and its surge on Monday led a tech sector rally. It is now one of the biggest weights pushing the market lower. The S&P 500 index is down 5.2 per cent for November, after losing some ground in October and September. “At this point, between the AI angst and the newly announced tariffs, it doesn’t look like the Santa Claus Rally is in store for us this year,” said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, in a research note. Questions about Nvidia’s corporate governance, as well as the influence of a U.S. president who owns millions of dollars’ worth of shares in the company, have added to concerns surrounding the artificial intelligence sector. Relief over Huang’s return as CEO is fading because of worries that AI might not produce enough profit to justify the large investments and stock values. That dynamic is running up against stubbornly high inflation. The latest update on inflation showed that prices rose at a more aggressive 3.8 per cent rate in October from the same period last year, and followed a 3.6 per cent rate in September. The data is from the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index. Aside from potentially stifling economic growth, high inflation could mean higher interest rates, with the Fed likely to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting to try to tame inflation. The rate of inflation is well above the central bank’s target of 2 per cent. The economy has been resilient, though, even as inflation squeezes households and businesses and consumers grow increasingly anxious about spending and finances. The government said that the economy grew even faster in the July-September quarter than previously estimated, with growth revised upward to a 4.3 per cent annual rate, the fastest in three years. Much of the spending that is driving the economy, though, has been from large tech firms building out AI infrastructure and from upper-income households. There are signs poorer Americans are relying more on credit to sustain their spending. Higher oil prices, fueled by the U.S. war with Iran and its impact on the world’s oil supply, have also contributed to inflation. The price of a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 3.5 per cent to settle at US$94.61 on Wednesday. The price has swung between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Energy companies mostly gained ground Wednesday, including a 1.1 per cent rise for Chevron. The wide-ranging and often uncertain U.S. trade conflict with much of the world also added to rising costs. The U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, the European Union and other trading partners after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down broader tariffs that were set last year. Businesses tend to pass along some or all of the cost of tariffs to consumers. Anger over stubbornly high prices was a factor in pushing voters to punish Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.87 per cent from 4.91 per cent late Tuesday. Markets fell throughout Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi lost 6.2 per cent as Samsung Electronics fell 9.9 per cent and SK Hynix plummeted 11.1 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8 per cent. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group slumped 14.8 per cent. U.S. financial markets will be closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. On Friday, the stock market will close at 1:00 p.m. Eastern, and the bond market will close at 2:00 p.m. Eastern. ___ Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press Business reporter Elaine Lai and economics writer Christopher Rugaber contributed to this report.

item.title: PM Carney says Pentagon’s complaints about Canada haven’t come up in Trump talks
item.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Pentagon’s recent complaints about Canada’s defence spending have not come up in his conversations with U.S. President Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Pentagon’s recent complaints about Canada’s defence spending have not come up in his conversations with U.S. President Donald Trump. On Monday, the Pentagon released what it called a “fact sheet” claiming Canada’s defence spending has limited its ability to contribute to the protection of North America. Asked about those complaints on his way into the Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday, Carney said Trump hasn’t brought up those concerns with him. “I can assure you that in my discussions with the president the United States, we’re focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently,” Carney said. The prime minister said Canada is taking responsibility for its own defence. He said Canada is on the front lines in Europe through Operation Reassurance in Latvia and is engaging with NATO partners to secure the Arctic and the Far North. Carney also said Canada is making “historic investments” in its military and getting members of the armed forces the pay they deserve. Under U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Trump administration has taken symbolic steps to upend the long-standing bilateral defence relationship between Canada and the United States. Hegseth last week issued a classified memo imposing restrictions on military co-operation with Canada on think-tanks and socializing. Defence Minister David McGuinty said Tuesday he can’t “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s recent criticism of Canada’s defence spending. “The amount of co-operation that we are pursuing together under Norad has not changed. What we are doing together at NATO has not changed,” McGuinty told reporters in Ottawa. “Our military-to-military co-operation has not changed.” Stephen Fuhr, secretary of state for defence procurement, suggested Wednesday that the Pentagon’s “briefing books haven’t been updated recently.” He cited Canada hitting NATO’s two per cent spending target earlier this year and its plans to buy new submarines, radar units and aircraft. “Our readiness has been not where we want it to be, and we all acknowledge that, but we’re making great progress and changing it. We’re buying new capabilities, we’re moving faster, more people are joining the Canadian Forces,” he told reporters before the caucus meeting Wednesday. “If we were to react to every single thing that came out of the United States, we’d have a headache. I don’t think they either know or appreciate how fast we’re moving.” A senior U.S. Department of Defense official said Hegseth’s memo was intended to ensure a unified objective during engagements with Canada. It does not affect military operations. The Trump administration official briefed a small group of Canadian journalists Monday on background in order to speak more candidly about Canada-U.S. relations. The official, who said the Pentagon is looking for Canada to commit to a realistic approach focused on military efficiency, cited the F-35 review. The Liberal government has yet to reach a decision on its full order of F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin — which Pentagon officials have cited as a source of frustration. Canada has committed to buy 16 of the aircraft, but the decision on the remainder of the planned 88-aircraft order has been the subject of a political review for more than a year. On Wednesday, Fuhr rejected the idea that the Pentagon was putting pressure on Ottawa to purchase the jets. He said Canada is still buying military equipment from the United States but is also diversifying into other markets and spending more of its defence dollars at home. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told reporters after question period on Wednesday that Hegseth should not dictate how Canada spends its defence dollars. But he also took issue with how the Liberals have been doling out defence spending and claimed the government is lining the pockets of lobbyists and corporations rather than helping military personnel. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026. With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa and Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

item.title: Loonie jumps as Macklem stays hawkish
item.description: The Canadian dollar jumped higher than it has in more than three months on Tuesday, as the Bank of Canada (BoC) signalled that it’s still worried about persistent inflation, which is also being felt ...
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: The Canadian dollar jumped higher than it has in more than three months on Tuesday, as the Bank of Canada (BoC) signalled that it’s still worried about persistent inflation, which is also being felt south of the border. With inflation running hot in both Canada and the U.S., largely due to months of elevated global oil prices, markets have priced in rate hikes from both the BoC and U.S. Federal Reserve at their next respective meetings. “The loonie follows the interest rate differentials,” Rahim Madhavji, president of Knightsbridge Foreign Exchange, told BNN Bloomberg on Wednesday. “If the BoC and the Fed raise rates in tandem, that generally bodes well for the loonie.” Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday in a speech at the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto that he expects “more pass-through to consumer prices in the year ahead,” despite the oil price relief seen in recent weeks. “This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence,” he said in prepared remarks, suggesting the BoC is prepared to raise rates for a second straight time next month in an effort to tame inflationary pressures. “The BoC with the speech yesterday basically has said: ‘Look, we’re going to raise rates.’ That differential has caught up, and that’s why the loonie basically repriced as a result of that interest rate differential,” Madhavji said. The Canadian dollar was up 0.49 per cent to more than 70 cents US in midday trading on Wednesday. Loonie supported by trade talks The signing of a new trade deal between Canada and the U.S. is another factor that would positively impact the Canadian dollar, according to Madhavji. “I think an announcement of a firm trade deal would be beneficial for Canada and would be beneficial for the loonie. It would be beneficial for certainty in businesses and investment going down the line,” he said. “The uncertainty and the lack of a trade deal is hurting the Canadian dollar. So, the fact that there’s been noise that we’re close to a deal, almost have a deal, looking for a fair deal; that bodes well for the loonie.” Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. have been taking place for months but seem to have heated up in recent weeks. U.S. President Donald Trump’s chief trade representative said on Wednesday that negotiations with Canada are continuing, but the two sides remain stuck on a few pressure points including around steel, aluminum and autos. “We want to make sure that North American trade in these products is beneficial to the United States. Obviously, there would have to be something that accommodates Canada as well,” said U.S. Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer in morning interview on CNBC. Greer’s comments came after yet another round of proposed U.S. tariffs, announced by the Trump administration Wednesday, targeting major trading partners including China, the European Union and Japan over subsidized production. Canada was not among them. “Until a deal is made, we basically have to keep waiting and seeing what’s exactly going to happen. We’re always one tweet away from some other type of news event, or increased tariffs, or a renegotiation or repricing of something,” Madhavji said. “So, you really need a firm deal, and people need to believe that the deal is going to be in place and that it’s firm, but a trade deal obviously benefits the Canadian dollar.” With files from CTV News’ Luca Caruso-Moro, The Canadian Press and The Associated Press

item.title: Investor Outlook: Groupe Dynamite price target cut to $83
item.description: Groupe Dynamite reports earnings Dec. 8 after a June selloff that followed a cut to its store-opening forecast.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Groupe Dynamite shares have struggled to recover from a nearly 36 per cent drop in June, when the retailer scaled back its store-opening forecast. Its next earnings report is due Dec. 8. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Mauricio Serna, executive director at UBS, about how the Canadian retailer stacks up against Aritzia and Abercrombie and what could set apparel brands apart in 2027. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: ROGER: UBS has cut its price target on Groupe Dynamite from $112 Canadian to $83, but is sticking with its buy rating. So, what’s behind the downgrade? Why does the analyst still see significant upside, and what does it say about the broader apparel retail sector? For more on this, we’re joined by Mauricio Serna, executive director at UBS. And Mauricio, thanks very much for joining us. MAURICIO: Good morning. Thanks for having me. ROGER: OK, why the change? MAURICIO: Yes. So our fundamental view on Groupe Dynamite is still bullish. We like the story. We think, you know, they have a differentiated strategy to drive very attractive long-term growth. However, we are taking a more measured approach on the valuation, just because we see increased caution on the consumer environment. You know, we see a lot of macro uncertainty. You know, we’ve heard companies reporting Q3 numbers in the last couple of weeks talking about a slow start of the quarter. So, just we believe at this point, a heightened macro uncertainty justifies a lower valuation multiple. So we think in this environment, you know, better to use a lower multiple than we would — than what we were using before. So we take him down the multiple that we were using to value the stock instead of, you know, using a 27 times P/E. That was our prior multiple. Now we think, you know, given the environment, you know, the market will probably be willing to pay for a good story like Groupe Dynamite, something like 20 times P/E, and that’s essentially the multiple that we’re using to get to $83 Canadian price target, which still implies a pretty sizable upside of over 60 per cent based on the current stock price. ROGER: So you still have optimism for it. Is that Spruce Point — the comments from them? Is that having an effect? Is that a factor at all right now? Any concerns with what they were saying? MAURICIO: So we haven’t really spent time, you know, looking at that report. Our sense, just on our checks, is that the brand Garage, you know, which is the key driver behind the story, maintains robust momentum, especially in the U.S., and that’s where, like, where we see the strong growth potential over time because it’s — it has a lot of white space opportunities. Again, I think it’s more coming from what we’re hearing from our own research, you know, about the U.S. consumer environment. We put out this note every month, and it’s our industry outlook. And in this report, it, it takes into account the response of a — 8,000 U.S. consumers and their view of the economy. And they seem to have concerns about inflation, about potential job loss. So these kind of caution, I think, it’s, you know, trickles down to — can trickle down, trickle down to stocks and sentiment around the specialty retailers like Groupe Dynamite. So that’s where we’re coming from when, you know, when we’re taking this more cautious approach in terms of the — in terms of the valuation and price target for the stock. ROGER: OK, it had that big selloff in June, but it’s raised its full-year guidance, improved margins, stronger sales. What are you going to be looking for next week? MAURICIO: Yes, I think next week or the week after. ROGER: Sorry, might be the week after. MAURICIO: The week after. Yes, you’re right. Dec. 8. For us, you know, we think they had a pretty strong third quarter. So we see a beat on sales and EPS, given the robust momentum in the U.S. As I mentioned before, I think looking into the print, it’s all going to come down to what commentary they provide about fourth quarter, quarter to date. You know, as, as I mentioned earlier, the companies that have announced so far have had some sort of cautionary comment, just because primarily November has been a slow start to the holiday season, and partly due to unseasonably warm weather. I think, you know, it all comes down to, you know, how trends industry-wise evolve over the next two weeks. But we are confident about Groupe Dynamite because it’s one of the brands that we see with very strong momentum, and we think that, you know, they can continue to point to, you know, a somewhat of a, like, a 10 per cent comp for the quarter, which is consistent with, with what they’ve been doing the last couple — the last quarter and their message coming out of the Q2 call. So I think that consistency is what could help investors get more confident about the company’s ability to deliver sustainable and attractive long-term growth. ROGER: And within the industry, things — groups like Aritzia, Abercrombie. How tight is the market right now? Especially if consumers are tightening the purse strings on their, on their wallets. MAURICIO: I think, you know, what we’ve seen in specialty apparel is there’s always, you know, ebbs and flows on the brands that are outperforming. You know, the consumers still shopping. I think it’s more of a game of, you know, market share gainers and donors. I think the some — the companies that you’ve mentioned are good examples of companies that have been taking market share. Because either the product that they’re coming out is resonating with consumer, you know, they’re investing in things like marketing, digital, AI, and I do believe that Groupe Dynamite probably belongs in that group as well. Just, you know, given their track record and their ongoing investments as they continue to expand their business. ROGER: And overall, heading into 2027, what are you looking for from the retail sector? MAURICIO: Yes, I mean, I think going into ’27, you know, we’re coming in, at least in the U.S., maybe like the — in the first half of the year, there’s a bit of a concern because consumers will be lapping, you know, tax refunds, so that, you know, has become — is a topic that a lot of investors are bringing up. I think we’re looking for companies that are able to show resilience because they have brands that, you know, are — have been building on momentum, that they can carry on that momentum. Also have very agile ways to react to consumers’ taste in, in terms of fashion, and, you know, that they continue to invest in, in growth because, you know, in, in specialty apparel and overall soft lines, that tends to be the biggest factor that drives stock performance over time. ROGER: OK, we have to wrap it up there, Mauricio. But always appreciate chatting with you. Thanks for joining us. MAURICIO: Great. Thanks for having me. Have a great day. ROGER: You too, Mauricio Serna, executive director at UBS. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Nov. 25, 2026 interview with Mauricio Serna are published with the assistance of AI. Original research, interview questions and added context was created by BNN Bloomberg journalists.
